title: A little lifting of the heart
word: A little lifting of the heart
hook: a small remembrance of God during the day is enough
tomorrow: what did a dying woman see when the room went dark?

segments.voice: Yesterday, when he failed: Lawrence confessed in a sentence, left the mending to God, and went back to the pans. The line was no fuss.

Two seconds between orders. Hands full, a line out the door, no chapel anywhere near. Does a glance toward God in a gap like that count for anything? One of Brother Lawrence's letters answers, and the odd thing is who he pictures. Not a monk on his knees. Someone on the march, sword in hand. Why would a kitchen brother write about prayer with a soldier in mind?
screen: `TWO SECONDS BETWEEN ORDERS.` → `DOES A GLANCE COUNT?` → `WHY A SOLDIER?`

segments.voice: Clue one, the size. Lawrence writes that a little lifting up of the heart is enough. A small remembrance of God. One act of inward worship. Clue two, the place. He says this holds even on a march, sword in hand. No candles, no kneeling, no hour set aside. The heart turns for a moment while the body keeps going. So the soldier isn't a strange choice at all. He's the hardest case. If a prayer fits there, it fits in a kitchen, a classroom, a checkout line. Clue three, its worth. Prayers like these, he writes, however short, are acceptable to God. In the same letter he adds that they don't weaken a soldier's courage in danger; they strengthen it. Clue four, what the whole book leans on. A bare tree that showed a young man God's providence. A clumsy footman. An omelette turned for love. The same work with a new reason. A failure met without fuss. Underneath every one of them is this smallest move: a heart lifted toward God for a moment, and then again. Catholics have an old name for prayers this short: aspirations. Today is our last day with Lawrence.
screen: `A LITTLE LIFTING IS ENOUGH.` · `EVEN SWORD IN HAND.` · `ACCEPTABLE TO GOD.` · `THE MOVE UNDER THE WHOLE BOOK.` · then, large: `A LITTLE LIFTING.`

segments.voice: Stand and walk slowly for a minute, around the room or down a hall. Each time you pass a doorway or turn a corner, let your heart lift toward God for a moment, a glance rather than a speech, and keep walking. Then sit for the rest of the time and wait for the next small lift to come on its own.
A little lifting of the heart. A moment's turn toward God, short enough for a march and, Lawrence writes, acceptable to God.
screen: `A LITTLE LIFTING OF THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this: a little lifting, then another, in the gaps between whatever comes next. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics call very short prayers said in the middle of the day aspirations, or ejaculatory prayers: a name or a single line, said quietly while working.

chat.meaning: Lawrence writes that a little lifting of the heart, even on the march, is a prayer acceptable to God. It doesn't wait for a quiet hour.
